newsitem.title: USA: Calif local governments join tobacco fight.
newsitem.headline: Calif local governments join tobacco fight.

text.p: Local governments in California have joined San Francisco in suing major tobacco companies to try to recover the costs of treating smoking-related illnesses, attorneys said Friday.
The move comes as tobacco companies are fighting similar suits by 14 U.S. states.
In June, San Francisco became the first local government in the United States to sue the tobacco industry when it filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court.

On Friday, San Francisco Deputy City Attorney Elizabeth Laporte said the suit was amended to add 10 counties. They are Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Sacramento, San Bernardino, San Mateo, Santa Barbara, Santa Clara, Santa Cruz and Shasta.
The amended lawsuit, seeking unspecified damages, alleged the tobacco companies suppressed and concealed information about the health consequences of cigarette smoking.
The suit seeks orders requiring the companies to stop the alleged targeting of youths in their advertising and to make public their research on smoking addiction and health.

In addition, Laporte said a second lawsuit was filed in state Superior Court by San Francisco, the 10 counties in the federal court complaint, and the city of San Jose. The state court suit, filed under state consumer protection statutes, seeks tobacco company profits and penalties.

"We welcome all the counties and cities joining because it shows just how important and serious this public health issue is. Even if our (state) Attorney General won't act, local governments will," said Laporte.
If successful, the tobacco companies could be forced to pay hundreds of millions of dollars, Laporte said.
The defendants were Brown & Williamson Corp., American Tobacco Co. and parent, B.A.T Industries Plc., Philip Morris Cos. Inc., and R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
Other defendants were Brooke Group Ltd.'s Liggett Group Inc., Loews Corp.'s Lorillard Tobacco Co., the Council for Tobacco Research and the Tobacco Institute.
A Brown & Williamson spokesman said, "The addition of plaintiffs doesn't add any more weight to the basic arguments in the case."

"We don't believe, at the end of the day, that the courts will allow the cities or municipalities to bypass traditional product liability law. We're going to vigorously defend this lawsuit and ultimately we believe we're going to prevail."
The other tobacco companies were not immediately available for comment.
